author: Bloch
name_in_asr: Vaisali (Hiuen Thsang's palace, Sammatiya monastery, Licchavi relic stupa, Asoka pillar and stupa, monkey-tank)
asr_identification: Vaisali = Basarh and adjoining villages (Muzaffarpur); palace = fort Raja Bisal ka garh; Asoka pillar/stupa/monkey-tank = Lion pillar, brick stupa and Ram-Kund in mauza Kolhua; relic stupa and Sammatiya monastery 1 mile NW of the palace, now level fields (old silted tank)
evidence: survey of c. 12 sq. miles mapped at 4 in. to the mile; Kolhua group a little over 2 miles NW of the fort; lion pillar, stupa N, brick-faced Ram-Kund tank S; excavation of the fort (c. 1,700 x 800 ft, ditch 125 ft): buildings back to at least 300 AD; c. 700 clay seals of 4th-5th c. (officials, guilds; Tirabhukti named twice); village names Kolhua = Kollaga, Basarh = Vaisali, Baniya = Vaniyagrama
quote: It is this group which I think proves conclusively that Vaisali is identical with Basarh and its adjoining villages. … We have here still the pillar crowned by a lion, said to have been erected by Asoka; … to the south an ancient brick-faced tank, now called Ram-Kund, which evidently is the monkey-tank … The direction and distance of this group from the old fort north of village Basarh tallies exactly with Hiuen Thsang’s account.
note: Agrees with Mizutani (07.03 Basarh; 07.03.04 Kolhua pillar) and with Cunningham's ASR identification (Besarh; Bakhra pillar); adds the Ram-Kund as the monkey-tank. Bloch could not find the relic stupa NW of the palace (Mizutani 07.03.03 = Altekar's 1958 stupa, in the area Bloch pointed to). Seals: Tirabhukti, not Vaisali, named.

author: Spooner
asr_identification: Mauryan pillared hall at Kumrahar, S of the main road between Bankipore and Patna City
evidence: ash stratum with polished Chunar-stone fragments in rows 15 ft apart (heaps over ash-funnels) = pillared hall; original floor 16 ft deep with wood; brick walls of Gupta date above
quote: Mr. Tata’s Excavations at Pataliputra … on opening up the soil at Kumrahar, we find first of all a maze of ruined brick walls extending all over the site … it became certain that a pillared hall had stood here.
note: Excavation fixes Mauryan Pataliputra at Kumrahar, E of Bankipore (Mizutani 08.02.01: 'between Patna and Dinapore'). The polished fragments here are hall columns, which bears on Waddell's Kumrahar pillar fragments that Mizutani takes as Asoka's pillar (08.02.05).

author: Spooner
name_in_asr: small rocky hill south-west of the old palace, with caves, and an ancient terrace beside it (new: 小石山 and 故臺, Mizutani 8.2.7)
asr_identification: ancient terrace = the artificial terrace found at Kumrahar (Patna); hill possibly = the raised ground on which Kumrahar village stands E of the terrace
evidence: terrace edge and mounds found 13 Dec 1913 at Kumrahar; village site higher than the fields; compared with the plan of Persepolis; Spooner's own translation of the passage
quote: Do not the Chinese pligrims tell us of the rocky hill he built at Mahendra. where he had his hermitage? … South-west of the old palace, he tells us, there is a small rocky hill. By the side of this there is an ancient terrace … If this is not our terrace, pray what is it? … The south-westerly direction from the palace seems a dificulty.
note: New proposal, not in Mizutani; Beglar (ASR 08) put the small rocky hill at Bhika Pahari. Spooner admits the bearing is wrong for his theory (it would have to be SE). Part of his Persepolis theory, since abandoned.

author: Spooner
name_in_asr: great Temple of Bodh Gaya; silver Bodhisattvas mentioned by the Chinese pilgrim
asr_identification: Mahabodhi temple, Bodh Gaya (as shown on a terracotta plaque found at Kumrahar)
evidence: oval terracotta plaque from Kumrahar Site No. 3 showing the temple with a seated Buddha, stupa finial, two standing nimbate figures before it, railing, and a pillar with elephant capital and a Kharoshthi inscription
quote: which seems beyond all doubt to be a picture of the great Temple of Bodh Gaya. … Are these the silver Bodhisattvas which the Chinese pilgrim mentions? They appear to be, so far as we can tell.
note: Iconographic support only: agrees with Mizutani and the ASR that the present temple is Xuanzang's 精舍 E of the Bodhi tree; the two figures match his silver Avalokitesvara and Maitreya at the outer gate. Not a location argument.

author: Spooner
asr_identification: Mauryan timber structure at the Bulandi Bagh, NW of Kumrahar, N of the railway (Patna)
evidence: trench through the Bagh: slanting timber frame 14 ft 6 in. wide on vertical planking, going down over 24 ft; 'primitive cast' coins, early pottery and terracottas with the lower woodwork
quote: the Bulandi Bagh, a raised area of mango orchard north-west of Kumrahar, on the north of the railway line … that it must be of Mauryan date seems obvious from the enormous depth to which it goes down.
note: Deep Mauryan woodwork (later recognised as the palisade) extends the Mauryan city along the Kumrahar–Bulandi Bagh line, E of Bankipore; consistent with Mizutani's Pataliputra but not with locating it towards Dinapore. Spooner refuses to interpret it yet.

author: Spooner
name_in_asr: five stupas which Hiuen Thsang tells us Asoka built (new: 五窣堵波); Nalanda 'university'
asr_identification: five stupas = Panch Pahari (Bara and Chota Pahari), S of the Agam Kuan, Patna — possibly all five inside the Bara Pahari mound; Nalanda = Baragaon ruins, 7 miles N of Rajgir
evidence: Bara Pahari excavation: wheel-plan stupa (hub and spoke walls) on an artificial plinth of kutcha brick, empty centre; second stupa SW of it; Mauryan polished stone fragments and large bricks; Nalanda: trench across Cunningham's quadrangles 2 and 1, north wall of the southern monastery found
quote: it was here thai Colonel Waddell thought to locate the five stupas which Hiven Thsang tellg us that Asoka built, and the identification I believe is generally accepted. … The position of the two which can be located suggests that possibly all five of the stupas which Asoka built are in this single mound … since Hiuen Thsang leads us #0 suppose that the quadrangle marked the No.1 on Cunningham’s plan was the oldest of them all
note: Confirms Waddell's identification of the five stupas (not in Mizutani's table) by excavation; Cunningham's ASR had put 08.02.03 (84,000 stupas) at Panch Pahari mound C. Also explains Xuanzang's remark on building on raised ground by the Mauryan artificial plinths. Nalanda (09.03.01) assumed = Baragaon, as Mizutani; the Xiyu ji used to choose where to dig.

author: Spooner
name_in_asr: Nalanda (Sri-Nalanda-Mahavihara); miraculous well inside the south gate
asr_identification: monastery Site No. 1 (southern monastery) at Baragaon = the Great Vihara of Sri-Nalanda; the large well in its courtyard is not Xuanzang's well
evidence: over twenty sealings of the Sri-Nalanda-Mahavihariya-Arya-Bhikshu-Sangha (wheel and two deer) from Site No. 1; Gupta official seal; royal genealogy plaques; large well in the NW quadrant of the courtyard
quote: the commonest of our types is the seal of the Sri-Nalanda-Mahavihivriy … Bhikshu-Sanyhasya or “ Venerable Community of Monks in the Great Vihara of Sri-Nalanda.” … I was at first inclined to trace a connexion between it and what the Chinese Pilgrim tells of the miraculous well inside the south gate of the main wall … This removes any possibility of our ;resent well being the one mentioned by Hsiian Chuang
note: Seals naming the monastery confirm Cunningham's and Mizutani's Nalanda = Baragaon. Spooner rereads the Chinese: the wall with the south gate is that of the Tara temple, not the enclosure of the whole precinct, so the precinct's single entrance is not fixed by the text (against Beal).

author: Hirananda Sastri
name_in_asr: standing Kwan-tsi-tsai (Avalokitesvara) image; stupa of Buddha's hair and nails (new: 如來三月剃髮剪爪窣堵波)
asr_identification: Avalokitesvara image in a miniature shrine at the NE corner of the large stupa, Site No. 3, SW of monastery Site 1; hair-and-nails stupa = the large stupa of Site No. 3, Nalanda
evidence: large stupa encased repeatedly, surrounded by many votive stupas, with temples at its corners; standing Avalokitesvara in situ to its NE; relative positions of other relics expected to follow
quote: recounting relics at Nalanda Hieun Tsiang notices a standing figure of Kwan tsi-tsai or Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, he saw, to which he attributes some tairaculous powers. Possibly this isthe very image spoken of … can safely: be identified with the stupain which the remains of Buddha’s hair and “nails, cut during three months, were, according to Hieun Tsiang, deposited.
note: New proposal for places not in the master table; cf. Mizutani 09.03.06 (精舍 W of the monastery, possibly among the caityas W of the monastery row), which Site No. 3 is now often taken to be. Nalanda itself as Mizutani.

author: Dikshit
asr_identification: Mahasthangarh, 7 miles N of Bogra (Bogra District), on the Karatoya; Bhasu Bihar visited
evidence: fort and mounds visited (Parasuram's palace partly dug by J. N. Gupta; Gokul Medh; Skanda Dhap; Gobinda's mound with stone steps to the Karatoya); Nandi prasasti (11th-12th c.) from Mankali's Kund; city limits traced to Ram Shahr
quote: Cunningham’s identification of the place with the city of Paundra Vardhana has been corroborated by references in the Karatoya Mahatmya, a somewhat late production, but has not been universally accepted by scholars … I also paid a visit to the remains at Bihar and Bhasu Bihar described and discussed by Cunningham
note: Reports Cunningham's identification (= Mizutani 10.04 Mahasthan, 10.04.02 Bhasu Bihar) as still disputed; asks for excavation; Skanda temple near the capital (Rajatarangini) as a test. No new evidence on Xuanzang's sites.

author: Dikshit
asr_identification: Rangamati (Chandpara, Jadupur), on the Bhagirathi, 1 1/2 miles from Chiroti station, Murshidabad District — doubtful as capital
evidence: Rakshasa-danga mound c. 40 ft high, 200 ft across; Rajbari or 'Raja Karna's palace' mounds at Jadupur; gold coins of the later Guptas Vishnugupta and Jayagupta; late Gupta sculptures
quote: the mound on the bank of the Bhagirathi at Rangamati which the Professor had identified with the Karna Suvarna of Hieun Tsang, should be excavated. … We have every reason to suppose that the ancient city at this site was in existence at the time of Hieun Tsang’s visit to Bengal.. Whether the capital of the Karna Suvarna country was at this place, as snpposed by Professor Beveridge is however a matter of doubt
note: Beveridge's identification (= Mizutani 10.08 Rangamati) reported; Dikshit accepts the site was occupied in Xuanzang's time but doubts it was the capital; mounds protected, excavation proposed (later excavation (outside these sources) is reported to have found Raktamṛttikā inscriptions, 10.08.02). Unlike the ASR (Beglar: Dulmi), points to Murshidabad.
